summary: Describes the standardization cooperation between IEEE Project 802 and the IETF. It was developed jointly by authors from both groups and approved by the IEEE 802 Executive Committee. It replaces RFC 4441.

plainLanguage.summary: IEEE 802 and the IETF make standards that often rely on each other. RFC 7241 explains how they can share information, review work and coordinate registry assignments while keeping their own procedures.

subtitle: How IEEE 802 and the IETF coordinate work across network standards.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802 and the IETF create standards that depend on each other, but they use different organizations, terminology and decision processes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how they can monitor proposed work, review each other's drafts, use liaison managers, and check protocol parameter registries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7241 is Informational, obsoletes RFC 4441, and has been updated by RFC 9141. It does not change either organization's formal procedures.

today: RFC 7241 obsoletes RFC 4441 and is updated by RFC 9141. It is an Informational document and does not change either organization's formal procedures.

sections.title: Why IEEE 802 and the IETF Cooperate
sections.content:
Project 802 of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) are independent standards organizations, but each uses work produced by the other. IEEE 802 covers local and metropolitan network technologies; the IETF works on Internet protocols including IP routing, transport and security.

RFC 7241 provides coordination principles intended to support interoperable technical specifications. It does not change the formal practices or procedures of either organization.
sections.plainLanguage: Each organization uses standards created by the other, so coordination can prevent conflicting work. Both organizations keep their own rules and approval processes.

sections.title: Different Structures and Decision Methods
sections.content:
IEEE 802 organizes projects in Working Groups and Task Groups under an Executive Committee. Voting membership depends on meeting attendance, although people who are not voters can still comment on drafts.

The IETF organizes work in Working Groups under Areas. Participation is open, there is no IETF membership, and technical decisions rely on working-group consensus rather than voting. The RFC notes that similar terms can mean different things: an IETF Area is similar to an IEEE 802 Working Group, an IETF Working Group to an IEEE 802 Task Group, and an IETF BOF to an IEEE 802 Study Group.
sections.plainLanguage: IEEE 802 grants voting membership based on participation at meetings, while the IETF is open to anyone and makes decisions by consensus. The two organizations also use some of the same words for different group structures.

sections.title: Noticing Work and Reviewing Drafts
sections.content:
Each organization should check the other's active work and alert its coordination contacts when a proposed project may overlap or depend on the other's standards. The shared new-work mailing list provides another way to announce proposals; IETF working-group charters can move through review in as little as two weeks.

IEEE 802 drafts use working-group and sponsor ballots, with at least 30 days for initial ballots and at least 10 days for recirculation ballots. IETF working groups do not ballot on consensus; useful review points include working-group adoption, Working Group Last Call and IETF Last Call. Liaison managers help keep communication moving but do not speak for the organization that appointed them.
sections.plainLanguage: Early notices and draft reviews help each side raise concerns before a specification is finished. Formal liaison managers keep messages moving but do not make decisions for either organization.

sections.title: Coordinating Number Registries
sections.content:
The IETF uses IANA to administer many protocol parameter registries, with allocation policies that vary by registry. IEEE uses its Registration Authority and also maintains identifier registries within Working Groups.

Ethertypes are scarce. IEEE does not assign a new Ethertype for an IETF protocol until the IESG has approved the protocol specification for RFC publication, except that early allocation can be considered in exceptional cases. When a document refers to a registry maintained by the other organization, its use should be checked during review.
sections.plainLanguage: Both organizations keep lists of assigned protocol values. Reviewers check the other organization's list before a standard relies on one of those values.

sections.title: Examples and Security
sections.content:
The appendix gives examples of cooperation: IEEE 802 work on management information bases with IETF expert review, and requests for IETF review of authentication and EAP work. The examples show how one organization can ask the other's specialists to review a specific technical area.

The Security Considerations section says that the document describes cooperation procedures and has no direct Internet security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: One organization can ask experts in the other to review a design. The RFC says its coordination guidance has no direct Internet security implications.
